## The founder-emulation items

1. **Who (practitioner `agent`).** YC-C names hotel groups with "call centers and central reservation departments";
   YC-L's video features front-desk staff at a Munich hotel. *My choice:* the reservation agent, central office or
   front desk, who sees the missed-call list. Segment: hotel groups in Germany with a central office or call center.
2. **When (circumstance, occasion, window).** YC-L's "After hours. During peak hours. On holidays." *My choice:* the
   occasion "reservation shift", window the last 7 days (calls come in on every shift; spec 120's "every shift" -> 7
   DAYS), Frequency 5 to 7 days out of 7.
3. **Who pays (decision-maker `director`, Buyer and payer, Purchase friction).** TERMS addresses the hotel group;
   YC-L asks to "book a 10-minute call if you lead a hotel group". *My choice:* the revenue or reservations director
   decides, the hotel's owner has to agree. Purchase friction tests "A data protection review of guest calls" (German
   hotels handle guests' card and personal data on the call); my choice, no source names it.
4. **Mechanism.** YC-C: missed calls forwarded to Codyco, the AI answers, bookings appear in the PMS. Compatibility
   tests call forwarding (the mechanism needs it); Adoption friction tests letting the AI answer in the hotel's voice.
5. **Cost, price, ability.** As in the table. Reading `budget` by the engine (a percent of calls against euros).
6. **Commitment.** TERMS and YC-L: the paid, money-back pilot at one location. The step carries its number ("pay
   €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel"), the gap-8 check.

## The respondents

No first-person account by a German reservation agent or revenue director was found in public (no HN thread; the
site's quotes are curated testimonials). **Every person is the author's invention**, no real person's name is used,
and each is built on the public facts named here.

Reservation agents (Parts 1 and 2):
- Lena Hoffmann: a trade-fair Saturday in a Munich central office; built on YC-L ("During peak hours") and the Munich
  hotel YC-L features.
- Murat Yilmaz: a check-in rush at the desk; YC-L's "peak hours".
- Chiara Russo: a group whose call center already answers after hours (YC-C: "Even with call centers..."); her pain is
  group emails, so Importance and Current solution go against the founder.
- Jonas Weber: alone on a Sunday desk; YC-L's "On holidays" / after hours.
- Aylin Demir: an old phone system that cannot forward (Compatibility only_with_help); the author's.
- Tobias Brandl: the sceptic who will not hand guests to an AI (Relative advantage negative, Adoption no); the author's.
- Elif Kaya: weekend abandoned calls seen on Monday; YC-L's "After hours".
- Daniel Okonkwo: rates pushed wrong to agencies matter more (Importance against); the author's.
- Mehmet Arslan: a vague story, GUESSED. Katarina Novak: a story chip, GUESSED.
- Florian Gruber, Nadia Haddad: gate No (no unanswered booking call in the 7 days).

Revenue directors (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3): Stefanie Wagner (6%), Andreas Keller (4%, below the founder's 5%),
Roberto Bianchi (8%), Ingrid Lindholm (2%, a call center covers after hours), Karim Benali (does not know his rate;
YC-L's "Free AI Strategy Workshop" and SITE's free test number as his ask), Petra Vogel (5%), Hannes Moser (nothing,
would not pay), Joanna Wiśniewska (10% at resort hotels in high season). The value boxes are percents of the calls, in
the founder's unit and period; the price picks are two codes, the pilot's rung and the licence's rung, each placed
against the founder's €3,000 and €1,000.

## Status today

Same idea (SITE, 2026-10-22): "Turn missed hotel calls into paid bookings.", widened to payments, invoices and
handovers; "Running at 15+ hotel groups" (the launch said 7); "€10k+ bookings written directly into the PMS". **No
public price today** (SITE and /faq show none); the €3,000 pilot terms remain the only priced source.

## Open (what could not be sourced, and the workarounds)

- **The licence amount** was never public. €1,000 to €1,500 per hotel a month is the operator's reading of the pilot's
  monthly rate (above). Treat the plan step's reading as a reading of that derivation.
- **Dollars or euros.** YC-L says "$5,000", YC-C "€5,000" for the same hotel; the pilot fee is in euros and the company
  is in Munich, so the entry is in euros. The market is DE, and the golden corpus's rule U (US only) is a note.
- **The "> 8 hotels" / "10 hotels" roll-out threshold** in TERMS and YC-L disagree; the entry does not use it.
- **Job titles.** Neither the agent nor the director is named in public; both are my choices (items 1 and 3).
- **The 5% is the founders' claim** for "the best" offices; no independent figure was sought.
- **UPFRONT_THEN has no "credited" or "money-back" flag**; the fee is a plain up-front amount (header).

screens.why3: I know from my pilots what a German hotel group puts in front of a phone AI: the DSGVO review of recorded guest calls and the PMS check.
screens.why4: It is a typing box with the hint's limits (up to four, 9 words, biggest first, not my own trial), and the only chip, Leave this out of the study, is the right escape for the founder's side.
screens.why5: The belief keeps my first and biggest step, a data protection review of guest calls, word for word, and the decider stays the hotel group revenue director.
screens.why7: The box asks for the right shape (buyer-side brakes, at most four, biggest first, not my trial or pilot), but the belief already shows 'within about 4 weeks' before I have typed any time, and the card says the time is mine alone and typed on the next screen.
screens.instead: Keep the question and hint, but show the belief without a time ('Most hotel group revenue directors would get through a data protection review of guest calls within the time you give next, or not need it') until I type it.

screens.why1: Right after I named who has to agree, it makes sense to check the steps a hotel group must clear before it pays for Codyco.
screens.why2: Data protection review, guest calls and PMS are all everyday words in German hotel reservations, and the intro is short and clear.
screens.why3: I know these hurdles first-hand from talking to hotel groups: the data protection check on recorded guest calls and the PMS question come up in every first conversation.
screens.why4: The data protection review is mine and right, but 'a check that bookings land in our PMS' is what my money-back pilot at one hotel exists to prove, and the third row is a long notice sentence sitting where a step should be.
screens.why5: My step is kept word for word, but the belief already says 'about 4 weeks', a time I never typed, and 'our PMS' slips into the hotel's own voice.
screens.why7: The belief carries a time I never typed, so the scale's edge would be nobody's belief, and the added PMS check is a step my own pilot removes rather than a brake on the buyer's side, so it breaks the card's rule on the founder's offer.
screens.instead: Rows: 'A data protection review of guest calls' and, as Keel's one suggestion, 'Works council sign-off on AI answering guest calls', with no added PMS check, the notice about my own offer shown as a hint under the list, and the belief left without a time until I type it on the Choose screen.

screens.why1: After writing the steps my buyer's side must clear, picking one and giving it my own time is the obvious next move before strangers are asked about it.
screens.why2: The words are mine and plain, but the intro's 'how long would this step take before it went through' reads oddly for a review, and the same hint is printed twice.
screens.why3: I know what a German hotel group's data protection officer does with recorded guest calls and card data, and roughly how long they take.
screens.why4: The data protection review is a real brake on the buyer's side, but 'A check that bookings land in our PMS' is close to what my own pilot proves, so it sits uneasily as a buyer-side step; the 'I'm not sure' escape fits.
screens.why5: The picked step and my 4 weeks are carried into the belief and the bar word for word, with 'under 4 weeks or not needed' counted for.
screens.why7: The step is the buyer's own brake, the time is the one I typed, and the bar puts the band starting at 4 weeks against, but the intro asks how long 'before it went through' rather than the step's own time, and the PMS row leans toward my own pilot.
screens.instead: Which one do you want to test? The person who decides is asked: if you bought Codyco, how long would this step take? (A data protection review of guest calls · A check that bookings land in the hotel's PMS) -- How long do you expect it to take? [number] [days/weeks/months] · I'm not sure

screens.why1: After who decides, the price and the purchase friction, asking what first step I want the revenue director to take is the natural last commercial question, and the frame says 6 of 6.
screens.why2: 'What's the first real step' and the examples are plain to me, but 'where would any money go?' needs a second read: the money goes to us for the pilot, and the real question is what the step costs them.
screens.why3: The first step I want from a hotel group is my own sales motion, the paid money-back pilot at one location in our partnership terms, so I answer from what I do every week.
screens.why4: The only chip, 'Leave this out of the study', is the right escape for a founder who has no step to test, and it does the same job as the card's 'I'm not sure'.
screens.why5: The belief keeps my step word for word: pay €3,000, money-back, a pilot, one hotel, and the revenue director as the one who decides.
screens.why7: My step is in base form and exactly 9 words, keeps every defining term (€3,000, money-back, one hotel) and the payer; the belief uses the 'In most cases {decider} would' form with no added 'now'; and the escape is the founder-side leave-out the card allows (the smaller free step this paid step needs is Keel's to write next, not this box's).
screens.instead: What's the first real step you'd want the revenue director to take, and what would it cost them? e.g. "pay for a pilot at one hotel" or "let us run a free trial"

screens.why1: Right after I typed my first step, Keel shows it back as strangers will hear it, with the belief it will test, so it is obvious why this screen is here.
screens.why2: 'Pay €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel' is how I and any hotel group revenue director would say it; nothing in it needs a second read.
screens.why3: A revenue director at a hotel group signs off on exactly this kind of pilot spend, so they can answer it from their own job.
screens.why4: The one row, the step, is clean and complete: it names the money, the money-back term and the single hotel, and nothing on it is odd or doubled.
screens.why5: It keeps my €3,000, the money-back guarantee and one location; only 'credited on roll-out' is gone, which the nine-word limit forces and which does not change what the director agrees to.
screens.why7: The step is the first real step in base form, at nine words, with every defining term kept and a belief that reads cleanly, but it costs the director €3,000 and no smaller free step was drafted beside it, so the soft yes can only be 'Probably yes' rather than 'Probably, after a 10-minute call first'.
screens.instead: Step: pay €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel; smaller step: a 10-minute call about one hotel -- so strangers see Yes, I'd pay €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel · Probably, after a 10-minute call about one hotel first · Probably not · No.

screens.why1: Right before the study goes out is the obvious moment to decide whether to ask people to take the next step, and I've just written that step on the screen before.
screens.why2: "Offer a pilot?" with "Yes, ask them" / "No pilot" is plain to me on first read, and "Pilot tab" is clear in context.
screens.why3: Whether I want leads for a pilot is my own call; I run pilots with hotel groups.
screens.why4: A yes/no choice is complete and distinct for this decision, and no escape is needed.
screens.why5: The line strangers would see, "Would you try this for real? Leave your email.", drops the step I just typed (pay €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel), so a yes here measures free interest, not my paid pilot.
screens.instead: Offer your pilot? People who say yes see: "Would your group pay €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel? Leave your email." — Yes, ask them / No pilot

screens.why1: Choosing who will interview my reservation agents belongs here, just before the study goes out.
screens.why2: The question is clear, but the hint packs in video, voice, credits and text message in one breath, and it says Keel records the 'voice' while my pick says it locks the 'face', so I read it twice.
screens.why3: Picking an interviewer after hearing a 5-second sample is something I can do as the founder.
screens.why4: Two distinct voices with previews and a preselect are workable, but nothing says whether either one speaks German to agents in Munich or Berlin, and that is the one thing I would need to know to pick.
screens.why5: Nothing of Codyco or my roles leaks into the choice, and my study is unchanged.
screens.instead: Who should ask your reservation agents in Germany your questions? Daphne (German, ▶ hear 5 s) / Saskia (German, ▶ hear 5 s), with the hint cut to: the interviewer asks aloud on video, every question is also on screen to type or tap, 400 credits either way.

screens.why1: After choosing how reservation agents are asked on the previous screen, it makes sense to choose separately how the revenue directors on the commercial link answer.
screens.why2: Video, reading and tapping, or letting them pick are plain choices, and 'directors' clearly means the revenue directors I named earlier.
screens.why3: I know my revenue directors: busy people at hotel groups who would rather read and tap than sit through a video, so I can answer this from my own market.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct and cover the real choice (voice, text, or both), and each has a short line saying what the respondent will actually do.
screens.why5: Nothing about Codyco or my roles is changed or leaked; it is purely a delivery choice and my pick of 'Read and tap' stands as I made it.
screens.instead: How should the hotel group revenue directors answer: Daphne on video, read and tap, or let them choose?

screens.why1: Once the interviews are set up, the obvious next step is to choose who receives the link, so it belongs at the end of the flow.
screens.why2: Each option says plainly what I do and what Keel does: name each person, pick a Contacts list, or post one open link where people sign in with Google.
screens.why3: I know who I would reach: the hotel groups we already work with and their reservation and revenue people by name, so I can answer this from my own situation.
screens.why4: The three ways to reach people (people I know, a Keel list, one open link for a group) are distinct and cover the cases, and no escape is needed for a choice of method.
screens.why5: Nothing of Codyco is changed or leaked, but the screen does not say whether these links go to the reservation agents or the revenue directors, though the screen before was about directors.
screens.instead: Who gets a link: the reservation agents and revenue directors? (People I know by name / A list I found with Keel / One open link I post where they already are)

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Did not hold' sits right under the title with the deciding card and its number (Purchase friction, 4 of 8 under 4 weeks), and the card itself shows bar 6 of 8, 2 short, so I know which belief sank the stage and by how much.
screens.why_b2: Each card gives its count, its n and its bar ('4 of 8 · bar 6 of 8 · 2 short'), but the kicker's '4 TO 8 COUNTED' made me stop and work out that different cards count different numbers of directors (7 on Existing sacrifice, 8 elsewhere).
screens.why_b3: Every card carries my belief as I checked it: the 5% of reservation calls, €3,000 up front then €1,000 per hotel a month, the director deciding with owner and finance agreeing, the data protection review within 4 weeks, and the €3,000 money-back pilot.
screens.why_b4: The only statement under the verdict explains who answered; nothing tells me what to do about half my directors expecting a 4-week-to-3-month data protection review, such as bringing a ready DPA and GDPR pack to the pilot offer or planning the pilot timeline around that review.
screens.why_b5: n=8 stays visible and the beliefs at the bar are only called 'Holding up', but Price at 4 of 8 against a bar of 6 is called a split while Purchase friction at the same 4 of 8 against 6 is 'Did not hold', so the same gap reads softer on price than it is.
screens.instead: Did not hold: only 4 of 8 directors expect the data protection review of guest calls to clear within 4 weeks (most say 4 weeks to 3 months); bring a ready GDPR/DPA pack with the €3,000 pilot offer and plan the pilot start around that review. Price is also 2 short at 4 of 8.

screens.why_b1: The deciding number is right there (4 of 7, bar 5 of 7, 1 short), but the status word 'People disagree a split' never tells me plainly whether my 5% held or not, and the run-on wording makes me reread it.
screens.why_b2: The axis plainly counts % of reservation calls per hotel a month and shows 7 counted, but 'your bar · 5 of 7' sits beside a marker at 5%, so I need a second look to see that one is a head count and the other is my percent.
screens.why_b3: It is my 5% of reservation calls per hotel a month, missed after hours, at peak or on holidays, the belief I checked.
screens.why_b4: The So line only repeats '1 short of the bar' and points me to the Price card; it doesn't say what a near-miss means for my 5% claim, such as that the groups whose call centre covers after hours lose less.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, Hannes's none-as-0 and Karim's can't-recall are explained, and 'a small group: a lean, not a call' keeps a 4-of-7 split from being called a result.
screens.instead: Not held, by one: 4 of 7 hotel groups miss 5% or more of reservation calls a month, against a bar of 5 of 7, and the two below (2% and 4%) already have call centres covering after hours, so lead with groups that have no night or holiday cover.

screens.why_b1: The numbers that decide it are right there (4 of 8 on each step, bar 6 of 8, 2 short), but the status word is People disagree, not did not hold, so I have to work out from the bar that my price failed.
screens.why_b2: The bands, the for/against labels and my edge at €3,000 and €1,000 read at once, but the second strip shows 4 for and 3 against under a 6 of 8 bar, and I need a second look to see that Hannes is missing from the monthly step.
screens.why_b3: The €3,000 then €1,000 per hotel a month is mine, but the belief drops that the €3,000 buys a money-back pilot at one hotel credited on roll-out, and it cuts my €1,000 to €1,500 licence to its bottom.
screens.why_b4: The So line only sends me to the Insights tab, though the quotes on this screen (four in a hundred calls across nine hotels, wanting it shown on their own numbers, wanting a free test number) already point to a concrete move.
screens.why_b5: n is visible, a small group is called a lean, not a call, and nothing is claimed beyond the 8 who answered.
screens.instead: Did not hold: 4 of 8 would pay €3,000 for the pilot and €1,000 a month after, bar 6 of 8. The 4 short lose fewer calls or want proof on their own numbers first, so a free or measured trial on their phone data may move them.

screens.why_b1: Too few to call sits right beside the number that decides it, 4 of 8 named my price or more with 5 needed, so I know the verdict and why.
screens.why_b2: The bars plainly count where the 4 directors at my price would find the money, but the strip's your bar · 4 of 5 (at least 2 in 3) with a ghost cell mixes the 5-person floor with the 2-in-3 bar and takes a second look to see that it is not a pass.
screens.why_b3: The line uses my numbers, €3,000 up front then €1,000 per hotel a month, but it is Keel's belief derived from my price, not one I checked, and the card still calls it mine.
screens.why_b4: Waits until 5 have tells me the count is short, but not plainly that I need at least one more revenue director to name my price, or that 3 of the 4 paying from an existing line is a good early sign.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible and a lean, not a call is honest, but 4 of 5 beside at least 2 in 3 can read as a met bar, and the rule line's or none names an answer the chart never offered while leaving out charged to the sites.
screens.instead: Too few to call: only 4 of my 8 directors named €3,000 and €1,000 a month or more, and 5 are needed; 3 of those 4 would pay from a budget line they already have and 1 needs a new one, so this leans my way. Reach at least one more director who accepts my price before I count on it.

screens.why_b1: The verdict *Holding up* sits right beside the number that decides it, 6 of 8 as I said or easier against a bar of 6 of 8, so I know it held, and only just.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four fixed answers over 8 directors, each bar is marked for or against, and the strip puts the marker at 6 on my bar, all readable at first look.
screens.why_b3: The title is Buyer and payer and the belief line is word for word the one I checked (revenue director decides, owner and finance director agree), though the bar line under it names only the owner.
screens.why_b4: *Plan for the hotel's owner in most deals; 2 of 8 could sign alone* tells me concretely to bring the owner into the pilot sale, and the managing director's quote (signed off after seeing it run at one hotel) backs the one-hotel pilot as the way in.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible and *a small group: a lean, not a call* is said, but *most deals* overstates: the owner was named by 4 of 8, which is half, not most, and the finance director I named was never asked about although the verdict reads as if my whole line held.
screens.instead: Holding up, just: 6 of 8 at the bar; half (4 of 8) said the owner must agree, so bring the owner into the pilot sale. The finance director you named was not asked about.

screens.why_b1: Did not hold sits right beside 4 of 8 under 4 weeks or not needed, bar 6 of 8, 2 short, so I know the verdict and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: Each band shows its count and whether it is for or against, the strip shows 8 people with the marker at 6, and the note that my 4 weeks is the low edge of the 4-weeks-to-3-months band explains why that band counts against me.
screens.why_b3: Purchase friction and the belief about a data protection review of guest calls within about 4 weeks are word for word what I checked, though the 'You said' line drops my 4 weeks.
screens.why_b4: 'Plan for a cycle of that length' points the right way, but 4 weeks to 3 months is a wide range, and the line does not say what that means for my 8-week money-back pilot or whether to bring the data protection paperwork to the first call.
screens.why_b5: The count line rightly calls 8 people a lean, not a call, but 'longer than your 4 weeks' takes in anyone who said exactly 4 weeks, and Hannes, who would not buy at all, counts for me with 'it wouldn't be needed'.
screens.instead: Your 4 weeks: 4 of 8 said 4 weeks to 3 months (that band starts at your 4 weeks), 4 said under that or not needed; from 8 people this is a lean. Assume the data protection review can run past your 8-week pilot, and have your data processing agreement ready before the first call.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "6 of 8 said yes · bar 6 of 8 · at the bar", so I know the belief held and that it held exactly on the line.
screens.why_b2: The bars count each answer to the pilot question over 8 directors, and the strip puts the marker at 6, so all three read at a glance; the first bar's label drops "at one hotel" but is still plainly my step.
screens.why_b3: The title is Commitment and the belief is my line word for word: the director paying €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel.
screens.why_b4: "Book them into it" is a concrete next move: put the six yeses into the paid pilot.
screens.why_b5: The count line says "a lean, not a call" and n stays visible, but the So line states "6 of 8 would pay" as fact rather than as what they said, at exactly the bar.
screens.instead: 6 of 8 said they'd pay €3,000 for the money-back pilot, exactly at your bar and a lean from 8; offer those six the pilot now and see who actually signs.

screens.why_b1: Each box opens on its verdict word with the deciding count beside it (Price 4 of 8 vs a bar of 6, 2 short; Purchase friction did not hold, 4 of 8, 2 short; Buyer and payer 6 of 8, at the bar), so I know where each line landed and why.
screens.why_b3: The dimension names and belief lines are the ones I checked, word for word, down to the €3,000 money-back pilot and the data protection review of guest calls.
screens.why_b4: The Price quotes point toward an action (show missed bookings on the group's own numbers, a free test number before a fee), but the screen never says what this means for my pilot or licence, and Purchase friction, the line that failed the stage, offers nothing to act on.
screens.why_b5: The counts stay visible and the 4 who never saw the friction question are named, but Joanna sits under 'the 2 who said no' on Buyer and payer while her quote says her managing director would agree quickly, which reads as easier than my belief, not against it.
screens.why_b6: I did not write that a group with a call center covering after hours wants proof on its own phone report first, or Andreas's sum that 4% missed across nine hotels does not cover €1,000 a hotel a month; both tell me the per-hotel licence has to be sold against the group's measured miss rate.
screens.instead: Purchase friction failed and none of the four who expected it to take longer were asked why. Ask them what the data protection review involves, and say plainly that the price objection is 'prove our own miss rate first', so I should lead with a measured missed-call report before asking for the €3,000.

screens.why1: On a link about the buying decision, opening with the idea I am asked to judge makes sense, and the kicker tells me that is what it is.
screens.why2: PMS, OPERA Cloud, Sihot and Apaleo are my everyday words, but 'your desk gets calls by rules you set' and 'in your hotel's voice' are vague; I would read them twice to work out that my agents still get the calls I choose and that it speaks as our brand.
screens.why3: We run a central reservations office in Germany and lose calls after hours and at peak, so I can picture this against my own week.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: It is shown on purpose as an idea and nothing leaks; the belief only repeats the first line ('take the calls nobody picks up') rather than saying what it would win me, which is thin but not wrong.
screens.why6: Heard once, seven sentences with 'the calls nobody picks up' three times and a colon-led list of three PMS names is a mouthful, though each sentence is short enough to follow.
screens.instead: Imagine Codyco, an AI reservation agent that answers the calls your team misses. Calls nobody picks up go to it; it answers as your hotel, takes the payment and writes the booking straight into your PMS, such as OPERA Cloud, Sihot or Apaleo. You choose which calls still ring through to your agents. The people building it believe it would turn missed calls after hours and at peak into bookings.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card, asking what share of our booking calls went unanswered is the obvious first question about what the problem already costs my group.
screens.why2: 'Rang out' is clear to me, but the three-way 'after hours, at peak or on a holiday' leaves me unsure whether it means the share of all calls that rang out at those times or the share of those times' calls that rang out, so I read it twice.
screens.why3: Our ACD report gives me the unanswered rate every month (about 6% for us), so I can answer from my own numbers.
screens.why4: One percent box, labelled in my terms, with 'I can't recall' as the escape; 'None' as zero makes sense for a percent.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product or the founder's own labels comes through; it reads as a plain question about our missed calls.
screens.why6: The question says well enough, but the three-part 'after hours, at peak or on a holiday' is a mouthful, and the trailing fragment 'A percent of the reservation calls last month' sounds clipped when heard.
screens.why7: It is a single rate on the founder's base (reservation calls) over one month, with a concrete verb instead of 'lost', so any figure lands for or against the founder's low, and 'I can't recall' is the one escape.
screens.instead: Last month, about what percent of your reservation calls rang out without anyone answering? [box] % of the reservation calls last month · None · I can't recall

screens.why1: Right after asking how many of our calls rang out after hours, at peak or on holidays, it makes sense to ask what a tool that picks those up would be worth to me, and I'm the one who signs for it.
screens.why2: An up-front fee per hotel and then a monthly fee per hotel is how our booking and channel tools are sold to us, and euro bands are plain to me on first reading.
screens.why3: I set and pay for budgets for reservation tools across our hotels, so I can answer this from what we already pay, not as a guess about someone else's job.
screens.why4: Both ladders are complete and don't overlap, 'Under €1,000' covers a tool with no setup fee, 'I wouldn't pay for this' is there, and the one escape fits.
screens.why5: The idea card is shown on purpose and the question only asks a price for it in our own billing terms, so nothing of the founder's plan reaches me where it shouldn't.
screens.why6: Each step is one short question with four options and the escape said last, the bands are said as euro amounts, and the two sides narrow to two bands, so I can hold it on the phone.
screens.why7: Every rung on both ladders is a euro amount per hotel for its period, with five bands in order, 'or more' on the last, then 'I wouldn't pay for this' and 'I can't say' apart; each ladder has bands on both sides of its middle so the belief can go either way, and nothing on screen shows any edge to be off the founder's low.

screens.why1: Right after I named a price for Codyco, it makes sense to ask where in our group's budget that money would actually come from.
screens.why2: Budget line, signed off, charged to the sites: this is how I talk about tool spend with our finance team, and it reads in one go.
screens.why3: I own the reservations and revenue tooling budget, so I know exactly whether this would sit in an existing line, be charged back to the hotels, or need a new line approved.
screens.why4: The sources are complete and distinct and the escape fits, but 'teams or sites' is not how a hotel group says it (we charge back to the hotels or properties), and 'a grant or outside funding' is an option no hotel group would pick for a call tool.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product, plan or the founder's own terms comes through; it only echoes the price I gave, though it drops the 'per hotel' I was asked about.
screens.why6: One short question, five short parallel options I can hold, and a single escape said last; 'the price you just gave' sidesteps reading the two-part price aloud.
screens.why7: Every option is a source of money in a tense that fits 'would', in the card's order: three for (existing line, charged to users, taken from other spend), two against (new line, outside funding), and the 'I can't say' escape apart.
screens.instead: You said about €3,000 to €5,000 up front per hotel, then €1,000 to €2,500 a month. If you went ahead at that, where would the money come from? An existing budget line · Charged back to the hotels that use it · A new budget line, signed off for it · A grant or outside funding · Taken from other spending · I can't say.

screens.why1: Right after I said where the money would come from, asking whether I can sign off myself or need the hotel's owner is the obvious next step in a buying decision.
screens.why2: Signing off on a per-hotel spend and the owner having to agree are everyday words in a German hotel group, where owners and management companies often split approvals.
screens.why3: I know my approval limits and when a property owner has to agree, so I can answer this from what I actually do.
screens.why4: The four run cleanly from me alone, to the owner, to several people, to not my call, each opening differently, and *I can't say* sits apart as the one escape.
screens.why5: The owner is the founder's role, named as the card asks, and nothing of the product's pitch or the founder's internal terms leaks into the question.
screens.why6: Heard once it is one short either-or question with four short spoken options and *Or say: I can't say.*, and *about three thousand euros per hotel* says well.
screens.why7: One measure (who has to agree), the fixed four in order with the tested role, the hotel's owner, in the second, for and against both reachable, and the one escape *I can't say* present.
screens.instead: Could you sign off on about €3,000 per hotel up front, then €1,000 to €2,500 a month, yourself, or would the hotel's owner have to agree? (same four options and I can't say; I said that monthly part too, and it weighs more in my approval than the up-front sum)

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I can sign off myself, it makes sense to ask what else stands between us and buying, and in Germany the data protection check is the obvious next hurdle for anything touching guest calls.
screens.why2: Data protection review is everyday language in my job here, where anything recording or handling guest calls goes past our data protection officer, so I understand it on first reading even if *of guest calls* is a slightly odd way to put it.
screens.why3: I have taken call-recording and CRM tools through our data protection officer before, so I know roughly how long that takes in our group.
screens.why4: The bands run cleanly from under two weeks to over six months with no overlap, *It wouldn't be needed* is a real possibility, and *I can't tell* is a fair way out for a purchase not yet made.
screens.why5: Only the product name I was shown on purpose appears, and the step is a gate from my own side, not anything of the founder's pitch.
screens.why6: Spoken as four options and then two, it is short and easy to hold, with one question and one way out said last.
screens.why7: Every option measures how long the review would take, a band edge sits exactly at the founder's four weeks, two bands plus *It wouldn't be needed* count for and three bands count against, the step is a real brake on the buyer's side, and *I can't tell* stands apart as the card requires.
screens.instead: If you bought Codyco, how long would your data protection review of the call handling take? Under 2 weeks · 2 to under 4 weeks · 4 weeks to 3 months · 3 to 6 months · Over 6 months · It wouldn't be needed · I can't tell.

screens.why1: A follow-up on the slow answer makes sense, but I was just asked about the data protection review, so asking what would take the time in buying Codyco half repeats what I already said instead of asking what slows that review.
screens.why2: The pick comes back as I would say it, '4 weeks to 3 months', and the question is plain German-office reality to me.
screens.why3: I know exactly what would drag: our data protection officer, the works council over recorded guest calls, the data processing agreement and where the AI vendor hosts the data.
screens.why4: A free text box with no options.
screens.why5: Codyco is the name from the idea card I was shown on purpose, and nothing of the founder's own terms or roles comes through.
screens.why6: Two short sentences, one question, nothing only the eye reads; easy to answer after one hearing.
screens.instead: You said 4 weeks to 3 months. What would hold up the data protection review of guest calls?

screens.why1: It comes last, after I have given my up-front price, said where the money would come from and who signs off, so asking whether I would actually take the first paid step follows naturally.
screens.why2: A €3,000 money-back pilot at one hotel is how vendors pitch to me all the time, and I understand it on first hearing.
screens.why3: I choose and pay for our booking tools, so whether I would put €3,000 into a refundable pilot at one property is my own decision.
screens.why4: The four answers are distinct and complete, run from firm yes to firm no, and are in words I would use.
screens.why5: The step keeps the founder's terms (the €3,000, money-back, one hotel) and nothing beyond the idea card leaks to me.
screens.why6: It is one short question with four short answers spoken as a list, and €3,000 reads aloud cleanly as three thousand euros.
screens.why7: The step costs me money, so the card asks for a free smaller step to sit in the soft yes ('Probably, after ... first'), but the list carries only 'Probably yes'; the measure, order, balance and the absence of an escape are otherwise right.
screens.instead: If it were ready today, would you pay €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel, or not? Yes, I'd pay €3,000 for a money-back pilot · Probably, after a free test on our overflow line first · Probably not · No
